div.p: On October 19, 2024, at around 11:00 p.m., Jane Doe arrived half-drunk (her own words, see below) at the Chi Phi frat house on the Cornell campus. What was her motivation? What is it that she hoped to achieve by walking into the building? We are going to argue that her motivation was religious. Religious? Yes. There is a tradition, going back 6,000 years to preliterate Mesopotamian civilization, of a ritual called the hieros gamosWe use the term here in a very loose sense. We will clarify what we mean exactly in Chapters 4 to 8., in which female priestesses had sex with high-status males (the King), as a consecration of the latter's fitness to rule. We are going to establish how this tradition migrated through historical eras and geographical locations to eventually find its way into postwar U.S. Greek-letter frat subculture. Anyone thinking at this point that this book is an attempt to shame women, or especially the Cornell 7 Jane Doe, by making her look like some kind of religious nut, should stop reading. There is no shame in being the victim of nefarious religion. There was no shame in drinking the Kool-Aid in Jonestown in 1978. We just need to better understand what we are dealing with here. Crying rape each time a frat group sex incident pops up is like crying gun control after each mass shooting. As an institutional damage-control strategy, such knee-jerk behavior is unfortunately somewhat understandable, given how the news-cycle work. For the rest of us these reactions merely amount to sticking our collective heads in the sand.

Frat party group sex is a symptom, not a problem to be dealt with in isolation. It is to be understood in the wider context of the increasingly severe signs demonstrating the intense mental suffering now ubiquitous among Western youth. Over the last thirty years, the psychological landscape for young adults has deteriorated markedly, reflected most starkly in a tragic surge in youth suicides. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the suicide rate among Americans aged 10 to 24 increased by 57.4% between 2007 and 2018 alone, solidifying its place as the second leading cause of death for this demographic. Concurrently, reliance on psychiatric medication has skyrocketed to unprecedented levels. Between 2016 and 2022, the dispensing rate of antidepressants and anxiolytics for adolescents and young adults increased by 66.3%, with prescribing trajectories for teenage girls jumping nearly 130% following the onset of the pandemic. This internal despair is mirrored by a profound social withdrawal. Contrary to cultural narratives of widespread promiscuity, Western youth are in the midst of a pronounced sex recession. Sociological surveys consistently reveal decreasing sexual activity, noting that young adults today are significantly more likely to report having had zero sexual partners in the past year compared to previous decades. This retreat from physical intimacy extends to long-term commitments, as marriage rates have plummeted to historic lows. In the United States, the national marriage rate fell from 9.8 per 1,000 population in 1990 to 5.1 per 1,000 in 2020. Furthermore, U.S. Census data reveals that only 20.3% of men and 30.3% of women born in the early 1990s were married by age 25, a dramatic collapse from earlier generations.See Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), State Suicide Rates Among Adolescents and Young Adults Aged 10–24: United States, 2000–2018 (National Vital Statistics Reports, 2020); K. P. Chua et al., Antidepressant Dispensing to US Adolescents and Young Adults: 2016–2022, Pediatrics (2024); CDC National Center for Health Statistics, National Marriage and Divorce Rate Trends; and U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey. When viewed against this staggering backdrop of rising mortality, chemical dependency, and relational isolation, hyper-sexualized collegiate rituals emerge not as a baseline norm, but as a desperate, symptomatic aberration in a deeply alienated generation.

div.head: 1.1 Police report
div.p: Between late 2024 and the fall of 2026, the Cornell 7 case underwent a convoluted legal evolution. Initially reported to Cornell University Police in November 2024, the incident resulted in an internal Title IX investigation but saw no criminal charges filed by the Tompkins County District Attorney at the time. However, after Jane Doe filed a sweeping civil lawsuit in September 2026 detailing a highly coordinated multi-partner encounter, public outrage surged. In response to the backlash and the reopening of the criminal investigation under a special prosecutor, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten issued a public notice on September 28, 2026, defending his office's original decision not to prosecute. Regarding the initial police report and sworn statement by the plaintiff, this document noted:

cit.quote: Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later.

div.p: It then goes on to quote the police report, reproduced below. This police report is a document of exceptional value for our approach because it documents the unfolding of a ritual which is meant to be witnessed, bragged about, sometimes filmed, but never described in print with near-anthropological precision, as is done here:

cit.quote: On the evening of October 19, 2024, Jane Doe walked the approximately one-mile distance from Lot 10 in the City of Ithaca to the Chi Phi Fraternity at 107 Edgemoor Lane to meet her friend Male Number 1. She had made plans to meet Male Number 1 earlier in the week and “had been texting [Male Number 1] that [she] was on the way.” Jane Doe described her level of intoxication as a “5 out of 10” when she arrived at the fraternity.

While there, Jane Doe opened one previously unopened can of beer. She and Male Number 1 “danced a little” in a way that “was definitely flirtatious in nature.” Male Number 1 brought Jane Doe to a “quiet area” and “asked how [Jane Doe] would feel about having a threesome with two male partners.”

Jane Doe “agreed due to how attracted [she] was to [Male Number 1] on top of [her] drunken curiousness.” When she learned that Male Number 2 would be the third participant, Jane Doe “remembered being excited because [she] thought that [Male Number 1 and Male Number 2] wanting to have a threesome meant that they were gay.”

The three engaged in a “threesome” involving oral and vaginal sex in a room of the fraternity. At the start of the threesome, Jane Doe described her intoxication level as “5 or 6 out of 10” and that she was “pretty ok with having this threesome.” The sexual conduct ended when Jane Doe “noticed that [Male Number 1] appeared really sleepy and was no longer fully erect.” She told Male Number 2 “[they] needed to stop having sex in order to make sure [Male Number 1] was ok. [Male Number 2] then stopped having sex with [Jane Doe].”
Male Number 1 said “he was going to take a nap and refresh himself” and “would eventually stumble his way from the couch to the bed.” While Male Number 1 slept,

“[Male Number 2] began to dry heave as if he was going to vomit. Jane Doe “began to take care of [Male Number 2] by patting his back while also waking [Male Number 1] every few minutes to make sure he was okay.” Jane Doe “was consoling [Male Number 2] on the couch and telling him that it was ok if he needed to vomit. [Male Number 2] told [Jane Doe] he was pretty sure he wasn’t going to vomit. Eventually, [Jane Doe and Male Number 2] would start making out for a very short amount of time.” While they were making out, “[Male Number 2] reached for the area near [her] vagina several times and each time he did, [she] would swat his hand away.”

Male Number 3 then knocked on the door of the room. Jane Doe “decided to let him in because it was his room.” She “opened the door” and let Male Number 3 in the room. Male Number 3 “introduced himself to [Jane Doe] and reached out to shake her hand.” “When [Jane Doe] made contact with [Male Number 3’s] hand, [Male Number 3] pulled [Jane Doe] into him and [they] began making out. While [Male Number 3] was kissing [her], [Male Number 2] began groping [her].” Eventually, “[Male Number 2, Male Number 3, and Jane Doe] would end up on the bed next to where [Male Number 1] was sleeping and [they] began to have a threesome.”

“[Male Number 1] would eventually wake up” and “said he wanted to take part and asked about making it a foursome, to which [Jane Doe] said ‘Hell No.” Jane Doe rejected this request “because [she] knew that a foursome meant that [she] would have to take part in anal sex.” Jane Doe then remembered Male Number 3 leaving the room.

A group of other men – later determined to be Male Number 4, Male Number 5, Male Number 6 and Male Number 7 – then entered the room. Jane Doe hid under the covers of the bed. Male Number 2 laid in the bed next to Jane Doe. Male Number 1 sat on the corner of the bed. Male Number 1 introduced the other males to Jane Doe.
Jane Doe had difficulty remembering parts of what happened next. She remembered

“[Male Number 7] said something very rude and mean to [her].” Male Number 7 apologized and “grabbed [her] face and started kissing [her].” Jane Doe “quickly backed away to stop [Male Number 7] from kissing [her].”

Male Number 2 “asked [Jane Doe] if she wanted to do more Ketamine.” At that, Jane Doe remembered “that [she] had taken Ketamine at some point on the couch with [Male Number 1 and Male Number 2] during this night” but she could not remember “where or when that took place.”

Jane Doe thought that she “had already done Ketamine once so why not do it a second time.” “At that point, [Male Number 2] poured a line of Ketamine on his erect penis, implying for [her] to snort the line. [Jane Doe] snorted the line of Ketamine, which was a heavy amount of Ketamine.” Jane Doe was under the covers of the bed at that point and “[Male Number 2] got under the covers with [her], where he again tried reaching for the area of [her] vagina.”

The males began complimenting Jane Doe and “talking about how pretty [she] was.” Male Number 4 “asked [Jane Doe] if they all could do drugs off of [her] perfect body.” Jane Doe responded, “Sure.” While the men were doing drugs off of her body, “[Male Number 3] and [another male] entered the room and said something like, ‘Ok we’re shutting down whatever the f*** this is.” Jane Doe felt dizzy due to a pre-existing medical condition causing dizziness combined with the effects of the Ketamine use. Male 5 or 6 (who apparently have the same first name) “encouraged [her] to stay seated as long as [she] needed.”

Eventually, “[Male Number 1] and [Male Number 4 ] ushered [Jane Doe] out of the room brought [her] upstairs to a small room.” Male Number 1 stated, “Let’s do more Ketamine.” Jane Doe “remembered snorting more Ketamine” and “remembered feeling extremely high.” Male Number 1 “said he wanted to have sex again because he wanted redemption for passing out earlier in the night.” Jane Doe initially stated that she was tired and asked Male Number 1, “What happened to just you and me?” Jane Doe could not remember how it started but she then engaged in a threesome with Male Number 1 and Male Number 4 involving oral sex and vaginal sex. She described her level of intoxication as “8 out of 10” at this point. “The threesome continued until at some point, around 5:45am, [Jane Doe] said [she] was tired and needed to turn in. At that point, both guys stopped the threesome with [her] as far as [she] can remember.”

div.head: 1.2 Previous cases
div.p: The history of the American college fraternity includes a record of group sexual encounters and subsequent legal battles, highlighting a tension between institutionalized group behavior, societal perception at large, and the law. Here are a few notable cases:

item.label: University of Pennsylvania (1983, Alpha Tau Omega fraternity)
item.p: A female student was involved in a multi-participant sexual event with members of a fraternity, later leading to convictions for sexual assault. Initially, university officials and fraternity members described the encounter as a consensual fraternity tradition (referred to as a train). This case established a precedent for how universities and legal frameworks interpret semi-public, multi-participant sexual events. It also solidified in the public's mind the picture of the frat orgy.

item.label: Florida State University (1988, Pi Kappa Alpha)
item.p: A female freshman was involved in a sequential multi-partner sexual encounter with several fraternity members, later leading to convictions. This case triggered especially intense outrage because the unconscious girl was later dumped in the hallway of another fraternity house in a clumsy attempt to misdirect the blame and potential legal fallout.

item.label: Georgia Tech (2013, Phi Kappa Tau)
item.p: A leaked email exposed a fraternity officer explicitly instructing members on how to engage intoxicated women in group encounters, utilizing terms like rapebait to describe activities that could be legally qualified as sexual assaults. This is analogous to the digital coordination seen in the Cornell 7 Snapchat messages (which reportedly described the presence of a female participant with graphic language). It differs primarily in that the Georgia Tech leak captured premeditated planning, whereas the Cornell 7 case captured real-time execution.

item.label: University of Nevada, Reno (2015, Sigma Nu)
item.p: The chapter was suspended after the discovery of printed pledge materials containing songs and instructions explicitly detailing multi-participant encounters with intoxicated women. Like the Georgia Tech 2013 case, it demonstrates the traditional and well-established aspect of the behavior.

item.label: Stanford University (2015, Brock Turner case)
item.p: A female student, who had passed out in a parking lot behind a dumpster near the Kappa Alpha fraternity house on the Stanford University campus, was sexually assaulted while unconscious by a student, Brock Turner, who was later convicted but leniently sentenced, triggering intense and widespread outrage. The victim, Chanel Miller, later revealed her identity and published a memoir titled Know My Name.

div.p: In many of these legal cases, defense attorneys cited the party environment and the porous boundaries of the fraternity house to argue that the events were consensual group sex or orgies, rather than crimes. The legal ambiguity surrounding intoxication and the presence of bystanders frequently results in prosecutors declining to pursue criminal charges, pushing these matters into civil litigation and Title IX university tribunals. Of course, this is only the tip of the proverbial iceberg. As we shall see in the next section, the vast majority of multi-participant frat party sexual events never result in legal proceedings or even reports to university authorities.

div.head: 1.3 The Reddit and Social Media evidence
div.p: Public digital records from forums such as Reddit, GreekRank, and localized university confession boards provide accounts detailing fraternity group sex. These posts are difficult to count with any exactness but they probably number in the high tens of thousands, if not more. These records reveal a consistent social pattern. The vocabulary used in these spaces suggests that the male participants in these encounters often hold high social status within their organizations—sometimes referred to by users as Chads. When these members organize a multi-partner encounter, the language used by peers often utilizes elevated or mythic terminology. The organizer is frequently described in terms of high reverence. For example, one user recounting an event on Reddit stated:

cit.quote: There was a guy in our chapter, absolute legend, who we basically considered god-tier after homecoming weekend. He managed to pull two girls upstairs and got three of the executive board brothers in on it to run a [explicit]. Half the pledge class was on door duty just listening. Dude is literally in our chapter’s hall of fame. He didn't buy a beer in this town for the rest of his senior year.

div.p: This account illustrates the social reward system. The organizer is granted god-tier status for his ability to coordinate the event. Another spectator account highlights the role of the audience in validating this status:

cit.quote: Craziest thing I saw? We had a massive tailgate and my pledge bro ended up in the downstairs bathroom with this girl. Next thing you know, the door is wide open and there’s literally a line of four brothers waiting outside giving each other high fives. Everyone in the living room could see exactly what was happening. Absolute legend.

div.p: In these narratives, the presence of the queue and the exhibitionism serve to manifest the group's hierarchy. By occupying the VIP Room or the upstairs area, these central participants establish their status. Other members, such as pledges guarding the doors or remaining in the basement, accept these roles while associating with the higher-status members. The use of mechanical slang (such as running a train or tapping guys in and out by a Conductor) distances the act from intimacy and reframes it as a group accomplishment, reinforcing the participants' status as Gods or Legends within their peer group. All this is consistent with the high status of the participants in the historical instances of the hieros gamos and the traditional role of the ritual in establishing that status.

While male participants are elevated to mythic standing, the digital record reveals a jarringly asymmetric reality for female participants, characterized by brutal, retributive slut-shaming. Crucially, this degradation is primarily executed and engineered by the female Greek hierarchy itself. As sociologists Elizabeth Armstrong, Laura Hamilton, and their co-authors demonstrated in their landmark 2014 study, Good Girls: Gender, Social Class, and Slut Discourse on Campus, slut-shaming within the elite university ecosystem is rarely driven by genuine moral outrage. Instead, it is deployed by female peers as a strategic weapon in rivalries and status contests. In this highly stratified Walled Garden, a woman's aesthetic capital is no defense against slut-shaming retribution. When a woman of high aesthetic value—often a near-Queen Bee from a top-tier sorority—voluntarily participates in a frat sex ritual, it triggers an immediate institutional purge. The fraternity men's elevation is thus inextricably linked to the woman's social destruction within the sorority system. Armstrong and Hamilton write:

cit.quote: Low-status women express class resentment—deriding rich, bitchy sluts for their wealth, exclusivity, and participation in casual sexual activity.
High-status women employ slut discourse to assert class advantage, defining their styles of femininity and approaches to sexuality as classy rather than trashy.

div.p: Digital archives—ranging from anonymous forums like GreekRankGreekRank is an anonymous online forum where users rank and review collegiate fraternities and sororities, frequently serving as a digital hub for campus gossip and aggressive social maneuvering. to college confession subreddits—extensively document the Machiavellian glee with which this demotion is carried out among the sorority communities. GreekRank serves as the primary staging ground for this public execution. When rumors of a high-status woman's involvement in a multi-partner encounter spread, underdog girls from lower-tier houses immediately weaponize the narrative to destroy her chapter's campus ranking. The rhetoric on these anonymous boards instantly strips the participant of her aristocratic armor, gleefully relabeling a previously untouchable girl with degrading, infrastructural terms such as the frat mattress or accusing her of taking the whole house. This digital schadenfreude allows rival women to watch a heavily armored elite peer voluntarily reduce herself to disposable tracks, thereby enabling the lower-tier houses to drag down a competing chapter's prestige while claiming moral superiority.

Inside the elite sorority itself, this purge is engineered with corporate efficiency through the chapter's Standards Board—an internal judicial committee that functions much like a Star Chamber. Direct internal rivals frequently orchestrate these tribunals, anonymously reporting the offending sister to have her excommunicated not out of moral concern, but under the guise of reputation management, branding her a PR liability who has damaged the brand. As documented in numerous college confession threads, these internal rivals exploit the frat rumors to create a power vacuum, eagerly calling emergency meetings to publicly purge the radioactive sister. By orchestrating this expulsion, the remaining girls publicly reaffirm their own pure, wife-material status. This creates a devastating double bind: the fraternity brothers use the woman to prove they are above the rules of the middle class, while the sorority sisters excommunicate her to prove they enforce the rules of the upper class. Ultimately, the female participant is entirely liquidated of her social capital, left as a ghost on campus—as one Reddit user lamented regarding her own sorority expulsion:

cit.quote: People who were my fam for life barely even acknowledge me now when they see me out in public.

div.p: Yet, despite all this, there remains a steady stream of female candidates for the frat hieros gamos female reputation-suicide ritual. How is that possible? One may invoke the information asymmetry generated by the yearly arrival of a new batch of freshmen on campus, but still, this tradition is now well known. It is hardly imaginable that even 18-year-old newly arrived freshmen girls would not know about it at all. The sorority grapevine no doubt informs them quickly about what the rules are. So, what is happening? How is the ritual still capable of exerting such a strong pull on generation after generation of female students?

div.head: 1.4 The Journalistic, Legal and Academic assessment
div.p: In general, it is fair to say that academic research on this topic has yielded poor results. The above-mentioned Good Girls: Gender, Social Class, and Slut Discourse on Campus or Peggy Reeves Sanday’s Fraternity Gang Rape: Sex, Brotherhood, and Privilege on Campus (1990, re-released in 2007), apart from usefully documenting the phenomenon, remain stuck in the heavy PoMo critical theory language of class warfare, upper vs. lower class conflict, and obsession with power. Beyond sounding scholarly, these clunky expressions, and the ill-defined concepts they refer to, explain nothing. In general, academic research in this field remains scantThe academic literature on this specific phenomenon is notably sparse. As Miranda Horvath and Liz Kelly observe in their 2009 study, empirical research addressing multiple-perpetrator sexual assaults is highly limited. Similarly, Leigh Harkins and Louise Dixon (2010) explicitly note the lack of comprehensive theoretical frameworks needed to understand the distinct group dynamics of multiple-perpetrator sexual offending. and of low explanatory value.

Journalistic treatment of this phenomenon often focuses on extreme outcomes. Consequently, the media tends to frame semi-public group sex primarily as a criminological issue—such as party rape or coercion. Journalistic accounts often highlight details such as drug use and leaked Snapchat messages, but rarely analyze the performative nature of these encounters as status-generating events. Official statistics measure reported harm, rather than the frequency or sociological function of these events.

Neither academic vacuous pontification nor journalistic sensationalism is helpful to the legal regulation of the phenomenon. A primary challenge is of course Consent Ambiguity. Fraternity parties frequently involve intoxication and lowered inhibitions within spaces characterized by porous physical boundaries, such as unlocked doors and multiple participants. What some participants might view as a consensual public exhibition, others experience (or later remember) as sexual assault. The legal system is primarily structured to adjudicate dyadic interactions between individuals. However, the group nature of a fraternity orgy can blur individual agency within a collective environment. When these semi-public, multi-person events enter the legal system, they are frequently classified as multiple-perpetrator sexual assaults rather than group sex, requiring prosecutors to evaluate intoxication, implicit social pressure, and the presence of spectators—factors that complicate the application of modern legal definitions of voluntary consent. This often results in the outright refusal to press charges, anticipating the impossibility to convict beyond a reasonable doubt, or sentencing perceived as overly lenient.

div.head: 1.5 This Book's approach
div.p: We argue here that the approaches outlined in the previous section are fundamentally inadequate because they fail (or refuse) to recognize the inherently religious nature of the phenomenon. What we are dealing with here is fundamentally an unacknowledged NRM (New Religious Movement) which escapes the traditional sociological investigation of such movements precisely because it does not declare itself as such. We will use the concept of Metaphysical desire developed by René GirardWe will use Girard's desire framework as presented in Deceit, Desire and the Novel (DD&TN), but will not refer to the rest of his output because we consider it a mere dilution of his original insight. In particular, we do not consider the scapegoat concept to be useful. to substantiate what we mean by religious.

In Chapters 2 and 3, we concern ourselves with the history of sex magick in 19th-century Occultism, its mingling with other form of elite sexual flouting among the British upper class in the interwar years, and finally how it entered the bloodstream of US Greek letter frat culture after World War II. In Chapter 4, we present a conceptual framework (the Kullaba-E-Anna model) which enables us to trace the cultural-religious phenomenon under discussion as it travels through history and geography until it reaches 19th-century Western occult circles. In Chapters 5 to 8, we present a series of historical junctures in which the model sheds light on the processes at work. These examples will provide us later on with points of comparison when we build our final interpretation of the Cornell 7 case and frat culture in general. In Chapter 9, we explain how Christianity built itself (and Western Culture in the process) as a patient pushback effort against the hieros-gamos-centric power dynamics discussed in the two previous chapters. We will then see how the downfall of Christianity in the West, starting with the elite, created a massive void into which the kind of barbarized hieros gamosWhat we have in mind here is Ibn Fadlan's description of a Norse funeral (cf. Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Risala) rather than the highly formal hieros gamos of the Ur-III period. Specialists have debated endlessly about whether these things constitute the same thing or even whether they existed at all. We feel that the material presented in Chapters 4 to 8 is sufficient evidence that they are indeed the same thing. that the frat-party orgy consists of found a welcoming ecological niche.
